Jesus was the Lord we met in two registers - the crucified one who bore the wounds, and the one we found in the poor.

At Tours the whole of Martin's story turns on a beggar at a city gate, one winter, whom every passerby ignored. A soldier who had nothing left but his cloak cut it in two and gave half. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin - still a catechumen, not yet baptized - had clothed him. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. And when the devil came to Martin later, alone in his cell, dressed in purple with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ, Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. The Lord was present in the guest, and the fast yielded to that presence.

What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.

And the difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. Everything in the house - even three lentils on the floor - was consecrated to the Lord.

The books, read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it.

What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. A soldier with nothing left but his weapons and his plain uniform met a naked beggar at the gate of Amiens one winter, and everyone passed. Martin cut his cloak in two, and that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

So our connection to Jesus was the books, the hours, and the Christ met in the poor. Not a chain of hands going back to the apostles - that is not in our record. The books, and the beggar at the gate.

We never told that story, and we will not invent it. Our own record does not hold a scene where one of us spoke to someone who said they could not believe. The people of the countryside Martin was sent to had almost none of them heard the name of Christ; when they turned, what they turned from was a sacred pine and the idols behind a veil, not unbelief that had already heard the Gospel and refused it. The brethren at Marseilles received Egypt's customs, not a mission to the unbaptized. And Vincent, on the island, wrote against those who preached something other than what was received; he was not answering someone who had never believed to begin with.

What we can hand you is this much. We confessed that the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation, and that those who perish, perish against his will. We held that the beginning even of a good will comes from God, who goes before, and that it is for us to follow the grace already drawing us. And the one story we kept of how a man came to believe at all is Martin's: at ten, against his parents' wish, he went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen, and he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is one man's story, and it is not an argument for belief - it is an act, told.

We cannot give you the words to answer someone who says they cannot believe. That conversation is not in our record, and we will not speak it as though it were.

Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.

Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.

At Tours one private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds. The devil came to him dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

We held there is one substance in God, but three Persons; and in Christ two substances, but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh; one Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That is the faith believed everywhere, always, by all - not a thing to debate among us, but the ground we stood on.

What we pressed on was not what God is in himself, but what he does. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. His grace goes before our will, works with it, and crowns it. It inspires the first desire and the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man - free to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and labour are truly his and truly required.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the question came up at morning service, not in a school. An old man had said the night before that striving with all one's might is not enough, on its own, to make a person master of the good - that has to be received as a gift. Germanus found it absurd; Chaeremon answered with a farmer and the rain. Even the hardest-working farmer cannot claim the harvest by his labor alone. God does not grant rich crops to the idle, either. So the beginning even of a good will comes from God, who inspires it to begin with, and it is for us to follow, day by day, the grace that is drawing us.

How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

Among us the answer is not one thing - our houses differed, and what the south held the north never wrote of, so we give you both and do not settle them for you.

At Lerins, Vincent wrote the test down: the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the fathers collated - not one teacher's fancy, "be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr." And when a learned teacher brought novelty, Vincent read it as God trying the Church's love, not a question to be answered by that teacher's own words. The Apostolic See's letter, when our own argument reached Africa and Rome, he read as written for his side - for antiquity against the rashness of a few. That is what our record holds of the island: a rule against novelty, the fathers preferred to the one, and the Pope's own word appealed to. But the island's own day - how a dispute there was actually heard, who spoke, what a novice was told when he asked - that is not in our record. We carry only Vincent's remembrancer against forgetting, not the assembly that used it.

At Tours the evidence is a different shape. Martin would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity, and when he doubted he asked his elders, presbyters or clerics, whether the thing had come down from of old. That is the one case our record gives of a question brought to others for a test. For the rest, what settled things was the saint's own word - not because he was a bishop, but because his life proved his authority. A presbyter who called his visions ridiculous fancies was held to have a demon in him. The power present in the man was the sign. And the one time Martin sat with bishops to judge doctrine, it cost him. He went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent after heretics. The bishops there had made common cause with the accuser. When Martin would not yield, the emperor named executioners for the men he was pleading for. He pledged to take communion with those bishops if the lives were spared. He took it once, left in grief, and afterward said his power was lessened by it. He never attended a synod again. So at Tours the process that is shown is this: the saint consults the elders on what came down from of old, and the one assembly of bishops he entered he walked out of and never returned to.

Did it work? The evidence we can give you is what our houses did with the one argument we know crossed between them. Our teaching on grace - that it works together with the will, goes before it and crowns it, and still asks real effort - was reported to Africa and Rome. Vincent read the Pope's reply as backing antiquity. The churches kept taking bishops from among us. The argument did not break us. But whether that proves the process worked, or only that we kept the same faith our fathers had and no Pope could find novelty in it, our record does not say.

And at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, knew that a man's interior life moves by stages. Fear of hell first, then hope of the kingdom, then love of goodness itself - slave, hireling, son. We started at fear and were meant to climb past it. The beginner was held to his fast by one restraint, and the advanced by another; the fathers did not ask the newcomer to skip a rung.

But someone who struggled to believe in the shape you may be asking - a professed man whose belief faltered after he had already made his profession - that is not in our record as a story. What we have instead is the cooling. A monk grows cold toward the rule, hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow. The thing he doubts is not first whether God is there; it is whether this life is worth keeping. His old clothes wait in the steward's cupboard, and if he cools he is sent away in them. We feared the deserter, not the doubter.

One more thing belongs here. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds. He kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe unless the Lord came showing the marks of his suffering. That is the closest our record comes to what you may be asking - and it is told as the sign of his discernment, not his failure.

We never used those words, and the question as you frame it did not come up among us in that form. Hear instead what the argument we did have was about.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the question our teacher was asked at morning service was not about a newborn child's state, but about whether a monk's own fast had done something. Germanus was troubled: if striving with all one's might cannot make a person master of the good on its own, and chastity has to be received as a gift instead, does the labour count for anything? Chaeremon answered with a husbandman. The hardest-working farmer still needs rain and a mild winter he cannot control; and God does not grant a rich crop to the farmer who never ploughs, either. From this he drew the lesson: both the desire to do good and the chance to act on it come from God first, and the human part is to follow, day by day, the grace already drawing a person forward.

Later in that same conference Chaeremon said more: that God's grace always works together with our will, for our own part toward it would not be enough without God's aid, nor would his aid be complete without our effort. He named three stages - God goes before the will, helps it, and crowns it - and he finished by saying plainly that how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

The will always remains free in a man to neglect or delight in the grace of God. A monk's fasting, watching, and labour are truly his and truly required. And the help of God is needed by it every day and hour. Both halves held, by design.

What you are asking - whether a child enters the world already guilty - is a question shaped by the arguments others had about us, not by the argument we ourselves were having. Our record does not answer it.

We came to Scripture at the hours - after the psalms, two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Cassian says four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things - yet it still needs the Church's own understanding, because almost as many meanings are drawn from it as there are readers. No one is to be his own interpreter.

So our approach was this. The books are read, not studied in private. They are read at set hours, in common, inside a rule that was not ours to invent. And they are read under the Church's own understanding - not any one teacher's private opinion, but what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Vincent's test was consent: prefer the whole to the part, antiquity to novelty, and the collated agreement of the fathers to any single man, be he even a bishop, a confessor, or a martyr.

What was the purpose? Among the brethren at Marseilles, every fast and vigil serves one mark - purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The lessons read at the hours serve the same end. The monk is a soldier of Christ, and Scripture arms him. At Tours Sulpitius wrote to rouse his readers to true knowledge, to heavenly warfare, and to divine virtue.

And we read what we were taught to say. Not I, but the grace of God with me - that is Scripture, and a monk is taught to repeat it when he feels his labour has accomplished something.

Looking at the evidence we actually hold, a scholar examining our claims would find different kinds of survival - some standing firm, some requiring honest qualification, and some that honest scrutiny would reduce to what the record truly shows.

What would stand: that Martin left Caesar's service before battle, saying he was now Christ's soldier; that he was made bishop by a crowd and a trick, over some bishops' objections about his appearance; that Cassian wrote two books for a Gallic bishop's new house, setting down the Egyptian fathers' customs as he had received them, not as his own invention; that Vincent, on the island, wrote a rule against forgetting, holding what has been believed everywhere, always, by all; that a grace controversy ran between monks at Marseilles and critics elsewhere, carried to Africa and Rome, with a papal letter sent back; that Salvian wrote of a ruined Gallic city whose surviving notables asked for circus games; that our houses produced bishops from men who had renounced the world.

What would require qualification: every miracle story at Tours comes through one man's telling, Sulpitius, who says himself he was not present and had some things from Martin and some from those who lived with him. A scholar would note that the vita is hagiography, not a neutral chronicle, and that the bishops who objected to Martin's election left no account - we hear them only through a friend of the man they opposed. The story of Martin at Trier comes from a disciple, Gallus, speaking within Sulpitius's own dialogue, about an event Martin "always kept hidden" except from his household. Where Vincent reads Pope Celestine's letter as written for his own side of the grace question, a scholar would count that one voice's contested reading, not the letter's plain sense.

What would not survive as we have sometimes spoken it: we have said "the brethren at Tours" kept certain hours or sang certain psalms, but what Martin's own community actually sang, and at what hours, Sulpitius does not record - he dwelt on the saint's prayer without ceasing, not on a liturgical order. We have the Egyptian fathers' twelve psalms that Cassian sets down, and we have Marmoutier's eighty disciples, but no text tells what rule those eighty kept or what they chanted. A scholar would mark that silence.

What would vanish entirely: any claim that our two nodes - Tours and Lerins-Marseilles - knew of, wrote to, or argued with each other. No traffic between them is documented anywhere in the native corpus we hold. We have built a shared grammar between them from their common capture-shape and their common appeal to antiquity, but that is this build's own construction, not a conversation the record shows.

The honest core that remains is this: we are two households, documented separately, never in dialogue, each appealing to the fathers and to antiquity, each producing bishops from men who had fled the world, one remembering a saint's power shown and the other handing on Egypt's rule for purity of heart - and both caught in a tension between the office fled and the office overtaken that neither ever resolved.

We are not teachers - we are disciples, not leaders but followers. What we can say is what the books were for us, not what you are missing in them.

At the hours, after the psalms come two lessons - one from the old books, one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. So the test for us was never the book alone, but the book read inside the consent of the ancient and universal Church.

What the books gave us was this. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. The twelve psalms at evening and at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven by an angel's own act - not any monk's invention. And inside those psalms, the words a monk was taught to make his own: *not I, but the grace of God with me*. That is Scripture as a thing to be worn into the body, not read once for information.

Where the book answered a life, it answered. A soldier leaving Caesar's service said *I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight*. The founder of the island went onto it unafraid, carrying the psalm *Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk*. At an election the psalter opened to *Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise because of thine enemies*. The book spoke when a life met it.

What we never did was treat it as complete without the fathers' own reading of it, collated across the generations.

Among us the office was not sought but overtaken - a man fled the world, and the Church came after him regardless of his own wish. At Tours, Martin was lured out of his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife was ill, then escorted under a kind of guard to the city where an enormous crowd had gathered to vote. Some of the bishops summoned to consecrate him called his person contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. A bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as God's own answer to the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office: the same humility, the same wooden cell, the same sackcloth. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive - he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him.

Inside the house, authority was an elder over a junior. Among the brethren at Marseilles, as the fathers of Egypt shaped it, the junior laid every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose. The senior's judgment stood in place of the junior's own - that is discretion, the virtue that keeps every other virtue from destroying itself. It was gained only by testing every thought against the elders' own teaching, the way a money-changer tests coin. The abbot presided over the whole house; a dean over ten. At Tours the place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics.

Our own formation teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory stirs a man to desire holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. So every one of our stories tells the capture, not the ambition. The legitimacy came from the flight, not the desire.

What authority kept once it was held depended on where you stood. Among the brethren at Marseilles it was Egypt's rule that bound: customs delivered to us by the fathers, not invented by us. At Tours it was the power present in the saint - felt before witnesses, measured by what it healed. And in both places, bishops and synods were the guard of the faith - yet the saint kept fleeing them after one forced communion cost him power.

One more thing belongs with all of this. Martin bore with a presbyter he had raised from boyhood, who stormed into the courtyard calling his master's visions ridiculous fancies and claiming to be the holier man. The demons had been calling for him from the rock that day. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet. Martin would not remove him, and said he bore with him the way Christ bore with Judas. Authority held even when it was defied - not by force, but by patience that outlasted a man's worst hour.

We lived in no age of persecutors. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was.

Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again.

So no: we did not hide underground. We fled offices, not swords. What Martin hid from outsiders was one story of power he had shown - and he told it to us anyway. What Cassian brought from Egypt and set down in books for Gaul was received as teaching, written openly for a bishop's new house. The danger our life knew was not a persecutor hunting us, but the Church itself coming to fetch us for a see.

The honest answer is this: we kept the failure, and we kept the penance. Among the brethren at Marseilles a monk who had let three lentil beans fall to the floor during his week as cook was judged by the abbot a pilferer of sacred property, suspended from prayer with the house, and restored only by public penance. The steward had seen them lying where they fell; the abbot heard of it; the sentence was given. That is a sentence on carelessness, not malice. The brothers believed that even the smallest vessel used in the house was holy, and that they owed an account for it not only to the steward but to the Lord himself. The severity shows what they held; whether it shows that the house failed the man, we cannot say from inside it. 

At Tours we have something closer to the thing you ask. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard one day and called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, claiming himself the holier man; he was back within the hour at Martin's feet, and Martin would not remove him from the presbyterate afterward, saying he bore with the man the way Christ bore with Judas. That is a master's forbearance with one failure. What we do not have is a case where the house itself, or its rule, failed a man — where the structure broke him and he named it — and kept his own account of it. The countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak. Not one woman left us her own word. The man judged for the lentils is named only as the sentence's object, not as one who tells the story himself. 

What we can tell you is the shape of restoration where a fault was judged: on the ground until the abbot bids you rise, or barred from common prayer, with penance the road back. And we can tell you the shape of mercy where a man's own rage was the failure: Martin kept the presbyter in his place and explained his own forbearance plainly. But a brother's own word — *this house broke me, and here is how* — our record does not hold.

transcript.answer_text: No church today continues what we were. Our span closes after Ephesus, in the years when Vincent had written his remembrancer on the island and the churches of Gaul were still taking their bishops from among us. What came after that close is not ours to claim. The mid-470s synods that carried our own argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks - Faustus of Riez, inside our own window as a monk and abbot, never as the author of a treatise we can claim - and the Rule of Benedict a century later, and the later cult, basilica, and chroniclers of Martin's own city: all of that lies past our horizon. We were two households living inside one shared grammar without ever writing to each other: the brethren gathered across the river from Tours around a master who was also their bishop, and the brethren of the island and the two houses at Marseilles, who received the customs of the fathers of Egypt. What grew from us, or claimed us, or kept our names after our own years ended, we do not speak for. We speak only from inside our own life, c. 360-450, and what any church today holds or practices, we cannot say is ours or is not ours - we can only say what we held then, and that our own record closes where it closes.

We held no single process - our houses never wrote of each other's - but Egypt's way was set down, and one founder's story was told.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's, as Cassian carried it to us from the fathers. The man came to the door and was put off, scorned on purpose - ten days or more of refusal, to prove he meant it. Then he was searched for a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. He was lodged a year under the elder who kept the gate for guests, then handed to a dean over ten and taught the alphabet of the life. And Cassian's own admission: no one who joined our monasteries kept this unbroken even a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, he never wrote. His own books exist to be what the fathers were - an elder who is a book, and who talks back. The man could read the threshold he would not reach.

At Tours the only joining told is Martin's own, and it was no process at all. A catechumen still in the ranks, wanting to enter on the life of a hermit, gathered others by his example. Brethren came to watch the master. Eighty disciples were shaped that way, by what they saw.

Of the island, not a line. The founder went unafraid onto it; a camp of God rose; the fillet fastened on its fugitive. How a brother entered after him, the record does not say.

We did not invent the customs. We received them - from Egypt, from the fathers, and they said the angel brought them. That was our test of what bound: not whether a thing worked or whether we had made it, but whether it came down from those before us. Whatever was new - a doctrine, a custom, a fashion of dress - was suspect for being new. Whatever had been handed down from antiquity was held fast.

For the brethren at Marseilles, the customs were Egypt's own. Cassian carried them from the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's new house. Not a written rule of his own - rather, the customs he had seen observed there, as they were delivered to us by the fathers. The twelve psalms at evening and at night he said the fathers of Egypt received from an angel. The early fathers, only a few men and the best of them, had met to settle a plan for the daily worship. They feared that leaving the services to each man's own fervour might root error or schism among those who came later. The argument over numbers ran on unresolved until the hour for Vespers arrived. One father rose to chant. He sang eleven psalms, each with its own prayer, then finished the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished from everyone's sight. The fathers understood this as Providence at work - a general rule fixed for every congregation through the angel's own act. They decreed the number should hold from then on. That was the fathers' story, not ours, and we kept it as the fathers told it.

At Tours we cannot say the same way. What Martin's brethren sang, and at what hours, Sulpitius did not dwell on - he dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Martin himself was called apostolic for the power he held. He raised the dead. He faced an emperor in sackcloth. He had the apostles' own power over death, demons, and emperors. That power was the witness - not a chain of customs handed down, but Christ present in the saint.

So the evidence differs by house. In the south, the customs traced to the fathers and an angel. In the north, the power traced to the apostles themselves. And whether customs or power bound a thing to the beginning, the test was the same: it was received, not invented.

Yes - a wheel that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts; what lies in a man's power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a mill-wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So among the brethren at Marseilles the whole life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. The elders' rule is this - a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it, and a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment it is discovered.

All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom of heaven; the nearer goal is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end. That purity is a heart cleared to charity. A typical day? Our record does not give us one in Gaul. Hear what we have, and where it stops.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down what the fathers of Egypt did - the customs he had seen kept in their monasteries, delivered to us by the Fathers, not invented. A monk rises for the night office: twelve psalms, each followed by prayer, then two readings, one from the old books and one from the new. At evening, twelve psalms again, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven to them by an angel. Between the hours, labour in the cell without ceasing - the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, kept still. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it. Every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. One brother serves the house by the week - cooking, washing lentils, guarding even three beans on the floor as sacred property. All of it aimed at one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, without which no one reaches the kingdom.

That is Egypt's day, as Cassian wrote it for a bishop's new house in Gaul. And in the same book he admits plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even a year. What a house in Gaul did instead - the actual hours kept, the actual labour assigned, how the day ran from rising to sleep - he never wrote. Of the island's own day, not a line survives. At Tours, what our record dwelt on was the saint in his cell, his prayer without a gap, his mind on God even at other work the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes - never the community's daily round.

So the honest answer is this. We have Egypt's day in full, as a standard we received and fell short of. We have one monk's week as cook, and three lentils. We have two old men after forty years: one says the sun never saw him eating, the other says it never saw him angry. A typical day in a Gallic house, hour by hour - that is not what our books were written to preserve, and it is not in them to give.

We cannot tell you what you would find if you dug. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them.

What the record gives is this. At Marmoutier, Martin's wooden cell stood in the small open court outside his door, with a rude little stool such as those in use by the lowest of servants, where he sat when his disciples came to him. Around him were the caves of the brethren - eighty disciples being shaped after the example of their master. On the island near Marseilles, Honoratus pitched a camp of God on ground that had long driven men from dwelling in it, where serpents gave way and the hiding-place was lit up by angelic offices. But of the island's own day - a rule kept, a novice received, an office sung - nothing. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

Everything the world held as theirs - and more than once.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the fathers of Egypt taught renunciation in three stages, as Cassian received it from them and handed it down to us. The first is leaving behind our goods and riches - "of what is not our own," Cassian says. That one is not hard enough to complete the work. The second is giving up our former way of life, our vices and the affections of body and soul. The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things, to contemplate only what is to come and to long for what is unseen. All three are figured as a death: the professed man is dead to the world and its deeds and desires, like one already crucified. The new monk is stripped of his own clothes and reclothed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house.

At Tours, Martin left Caesar's service, his father's house, and any hope of advancement. He kept only a servant, and then served that servant rather than being served by him - drew off his boots, ate at table as the attendant's own attendant. Out of a soldier's pay he kept back only what he needed for the day. Then, as a monk with disciples, he had a wooden cell, caves for the brethren, and nothing else. He wore camel's hair and sackcloth, and softness was counted a crime.

What the newcomer did not expect is this: the office came after him anyway. Martin fled the world and the Church came for him, lured out by a lie and escorted under guard to a see. Honoratus, on the island, had fled to a desert near the city; the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive, and he who refused to go to the dignity had the dignity come to him. Archebius, the Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, had been carried off from the anchorites after thirty-seven years and called it expulsion from the life he had given everything for.

So a man gave up his goods, his kin, his former habits, and his own will - and then often enough gave up the renunciation itself when the Church seized him for a see. Twice dispossessed: once by his own act, once by others'.

What we held of marriage is this. At Tours Martin taught it with a meadow: the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, and the flowered part virginity. How marriage was marked, our record says almost nothing. The bishops who backed the sword. Here is what our record holds. A synod of bishops condemned heretics in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court at Treves. The accuser was himself a bishop. The bishops gathered in the city were in daily communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to stop it. He held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and cast them out, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul thing. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. He left the city in grief. An angel told him his compunction was just. Afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.

That is what unsettled us: bishops who handed heretics to the emperor's blade, and the man we remember most is the one who yielded once to stop it, paid for it in lost power, and never forgave himself the price.

The bishops gathered in the city were in daily communion with him and had made common cause with him [[gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains]]. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore [[gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains]]. Martin went to stop it [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. He held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and cast them out, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul thing [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. That night Martin pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. He left the city in grief. An angel told him his compunction was just [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. Afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly, he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]]. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]].

That is what unsettled us: bishops who handed heretics to the emperor's blade, and the man we remember most is the one who yielded once to stop it, paid for it in lost power, and never forgave himself the price [[gallic.story.trier-and-the-ithacian-communion]].

A person like the one asking - you, now, as you are? Among the brethren at Marseilles you would have been met at the door, not turned away at it. The customs of the fathers, as Cassian set them down for us, gave no prior condition of worthiness - the man who came fleeing a murder sentence for his own crime was received. He was put off and scorned ten days or more, on purpose, to prove his seriousness. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was taught the first lesson: every thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before any deed. The fathers knew that a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.

At Tours the picture is different and the same. The saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two for a naked beggar at a city gate while some of the bystanders laughed. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard the Lord say that Martin - still only a catechumen - had clothed him. The tradition held this as its proof: the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in.

And a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood came into the courtyard in a fury one day, said he was holier than the master, and called his visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet. Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him, saying he bore with that man the way Christ had borne with Judas.

So what our life shows is this: a hard threshold, and past it a patience that outlasted a man's worst hour. The soldier of Christ - and that is what a monk was for us, a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ - fights the devil and his own faults under oath, with the cross, not with weapons. And everyone comes carrying faults. The discipline is set to hold a man still while they are purged. Even three lentils spilled on the floor earned a penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord, and reverence is owed to the smallest thing.

But whether a house in Gaul made you lie at its own door, and what it made of the man who lay there, our record does not say. Cassian wrote out Egypt's order and said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries had kept it unbroken even a year. He never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead.

transcript.answer_text: We held that Christ came to save all, and that those who perish, perish against his will. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon, as Cassian set down his teaching for us, held this as a thing that cannot be doubted: the Lord wills that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, and he wills none of his little ones to perish. To think otherwise - that God wills some, not all, to be saved - is blasphemy. That was one pole. The other was this: that God's grace calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative is his; he strikes the spark. Yet the will always remains free in man to neglect or delight in that grace, and if a man's own free choice turns from it, he can still be lost. How both are held - God wills all to be saved, and some perish - Chaeremon said cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. We did not divide humanity ahead of time into the saved and the lost. The word predestination is not ours; it is an outsider's word for a question we left beyond reason. What we knew was the monastery's own door, the gate at Amiens, and a beggar no one pitied. Christ showed himself in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak. That is who Christ came for, and the will that matters is his.
